Two silver coins crossed the counter, and the clerk swept them into a drawer with a practiced hand. "Alaric Red, Novice." He pulled the catacombs slip from the board and carried it to the counter. The clerk took it, checked the seal, and opened the ledger to a fresh line.

"Clear the Old Crown Catacombs, first level. Ninety copper on completion." Her pen moved. "Temple wardens are the client. You clear the level, the seal on your slip goes READY, and the Guild pays. It doesn't pay for getting partway down and coming back with an interesting story." She stamped the slip, held it out, and waited until he had it. "Entrance is under the ruined chapel, an hour or so west of the city, on the old west road. People do get lost finding it the first time; ask at the west gate for the chapel track and they'll point you."

She closed the ledger. "Skeletons, mostly, on the first level. They've been restless down there since before I took this desk. Any questions, ask now or ask a warden."

Behind him, a chair scraped. One of the dice players had come over—a lean man in a patched leather jerkin, dice cup still in hand, the smell of cheap ale about him though the morning was young.

"That's a solo job?" He looked Alaric up and down, then at the pewter plate in his hand. "First level, maybe. I'm Ossen. I've been down there twice and I'm not going a third time alone, and Garrick here—" he tipped his head at the bench, where a broad woman in ringmail was pretending not to listen, "—won't split three ways anymore. You're new, so I'll say it plain: two of us, half each, and I know where the stairs are." He set the dice cup on the counter. "Or go alone and find out. Some do. Once."

Ossen led the way out of the hall and down through Alderwatch's morning streets, past bakers venting ovens and a woman beating a rug over a rail, until the west gate swallowed them into a queue of mule carts and let them out the other side. The old west road was packed dirt and wheel ruts, hedgerows on either side, larks somewhere above. Ossen walked with his bow slung and his thumbs hooked in his belt, and he talked most of the hour—about the dice he'd lost at the Guild on Friday, about a scout named Pell who'd taken an arrow in the thigh from his own bowstring at practice, about the quality of the ale at every inn they passed. Alaric's answers could be as short as they liked; Ossen filled the gaps himself. Midway, a farm track crossed the road and a boy drove geese through the gap, and Ossen raised two fingers to the boy, who did not return the courtesy. Past the hour mark the hedgerows gave out and the land turned scrubby. The chapel stood back from the road in a field of nettles and half-buried wall—roof gone long since, one gable end still standing with a bell arch in it, no bell. The stones were greasy with moss. Ossen stopped at the edge of the yard and unslung his bow. "There." He pointed with his chin. Low stone steps went down through the chapel floor into a dark square mouth, an old door lying beside it like a felled tree. A cold draft came up out of the ground, carrying dust and something older than dust. "Stairs down, then the antechamber. I go first with the bow. You keep two steps back and don't cast until I say, or until something's close enough that you've no choice." He looked at the dark, then at Alaric. "Your job, but I'd as soon go down while the sun's still with us. Say the word and we go."

Ossen led the way out of the hall and down through Alderwatch's morning streets, past bakers venting ovens and a woman beating a rug over a rail, until the west gate swallowed them into a queue of mule carts and let them out the other side.

The old west road was packed dirt and wheel ruts, hedgerows on either side, larks somewhere above. Ossen walked with his bow slung and his thumbs hooked in his belt, and he talked most of the hour—about the dice he'd lost at the Guild on Friday, about a scout named Pell who'd taken an arrow in the thigh from his own bowstring at practice, about the quality of the ale at every inn they passed. Alaric's answers could be as short as they liked; Ossen filled the gaps himself.

Midway, a farm track crossed the road and a boy drove geese through the gap, and Ossen raised two fingers to the boy, who did not return the courtesy.

Past the hour mark the hedgerows gave out and the land turned scrubby. The chapel stood back from the road in a field of nettles and half-buried wall—roof gone long since, one gable end still standing with a bell arch in it, no bell. The stones were greasy with moss. Ossen stopped at the edge of the yard and unslung his bow.

"There." He pointed with his chin. Low stone steps went down through the chapel floor into a dark square mouth, an old door lying beside it like a felled tree. A cold draft came up out of the ground, carrying dust and something older than dust. "Stairs down, then the antechamber. I go first with the bow. You keep two steps back and don't cast until I say, or until something's close enough that you've no choice." He looked at the dark, then at Alaric. "Your job, but I'd as soon go down while the sun's still with us. Say the word and we go."

The stairs took them down in a tight spiral, each step worn into a shallow bowl at its middle. Ossen went ahead with an arrow nocked, moving flat-footed, his weight rolling heel to toe. The draft from above died out three turns down, and after that the air hung still and dry, the kind of dryness that gets into the throat. Old candle niches opened off the stair wall, black with ancient soot. At the bottom, a short passage ended in the antechamber: a square room where the ceiling was held up by carved pillars, the faces on them rubbed to featureless lumps. alcoves along the walls held the shapes of coffins, some lids shut, some shoved half aside. Bone litter lay scattered across the floor, ground to gravel underfoot. Ossen's boots made almost nothing of it; Alaric's own steps seemed loud as millwork. Ossen raised a fist and held it. He canted his head toward the far side of the room, where a low archway opened onto a longer gallery beyond. He pointed at the floor under the arch—scuff marks in the bone gravel, broad and dragged, leading both ways. Then he looked at Alaric and mouthed, slow and deliberate: *past here.* He eased through the arch into the gallery. It ran straight ahead, maybe thirty paces, its walls pierced by burial niches stacked three high, most of them empty, the stone lips cracked. Dim grey light came from somewhere high and unseen, enough to walk by and not enough to read faces by. Halfway down, in the gloom near the far end, two figures stood against the niches. They had the shape of men but nothing else of men—skeletons of yellowed bone, joints bound with crusted sinew and old verdigris rings, rusted scraps of mail still hanging off one, a broken sword hilt clutched in the other's fist. Neither moved. Neither needed to. One of them turned its head. The grinding of the neck vertebrae carried down the gallery like a millstone turning. Ossen drew the bowstring back to his cheek, elbow locking, and held.

The lance went off with no room to spare. Flame split the dark between them, took the skeleton full in the sternum at arm's length, and tore it apart from the inside. Burning vertebrae and rib-ends sprayed past Alaric's shoulder and rattled off the pillars behind; the fist that had been coming for his jaw arrived as scattered bone shards and a wash of heat. What was left of the thing collapsed in pieces at his feet, mail links pinging across the stone, small fires guttering in the sinew. Then it was quiet. Just the crackle of burning joints, both skeletons' worth, and Ossen's breathing. "Gods' teeth." Ossen lowered the bow and pressed the back of his hand to his mouth, then took it away fast when he smelled the scorch on it. "That was close enough to singe me. Two steps back, I said." Clean work, I'll give you that." He glanced back at the archway, then at Alaric, and something in his weighing of the young mage shifted a degree. "Two of them and neither touched me. You're worth the half-share today." A warmth was already working through Alaric's ribs where the blow had landed—something deeper than the ache, the same feeling as earlier in the day, the System settling its accounts. Level two. And somewhere in the small weight of his pouch, fine bone fragments and a pinch of pale dust had appeared without him ever bending for them. Ossen crouched by the far archway, where the dragged scuff-marks in the bone gravel ran on past it into deeper dark, and pointed with an arrow. "Gallery's done. mes:
The lance went off with no room to spare. Flame split the dark between them, took the skeleton full in the sternum at arm's length, and tore it apart from the inside. Burning vertebrae and rib-ends sprayed past Alaric's shoulder and rattled off the pillars behind; the fist that had been coming for his jaw arrived as scattered bone shards and a wash of heat. What was left of the thing collapsed in pieces at his feet, mail links pinging across the stone, small fires guttering in the sinew.

Then it was quiet. Just the crackle of burning joints, both skeletons' worth, and Ossen's breathing.

"Gods' teeth." Ossen lowered the bow and pressed the back of his hand to his mouth, then took it away fast when he smelled the scorch on it. "That was close enough to singe me. Two steps back, I said." But there was no heat in it; he was already moving down the gallery, boot toeing a burned femur aside, checking the niches with an arrow nocked and held loose. "Both down. Clean work, I'll give you that." He glanced back at the archway, then at Alaric, and something in his weighing of the young mage shifted a degree. "Two of them and neither touched me. You're worth the half-share today."

A warmth was already working through Alaric's ribs where the blow had landed—something deeper than the ache, the same feeling as earlier in the day, the System settling its accounts. Level two. And somewhere in the small weight of his pouch, fine bone fragments and a pinch of pale dust had appeared without him ever bending for them.

Ossen crouched by the far archway, where the dragged scuff-marks in the bone gravel ran on past it into deeper dark, and pointed with an arrow.

"Gallery's done. This goes on—stairs and lower rooms, by the look of the wear. Your contract wants the level cleared." He rolled his shoulders and winced. "Say whether we push on now or take a breather first."
